chapter.title: Reach the top, and the last line

cards.body: What was on the last slide of the best talk you remember? Almost never 'thank you'. On a hike you don't stop ten metres below the summit to thank everyone for walking. You climb the last bit, turn them round and **show them the view**: what life looks like with your idea, and one line that names it.
cards.simpler: Think of the best talk you remember. What was on its last slide? Almost never 'thank you'. On a hike, you don't stop ten metres below the top to thank everyone for walking. You climb the last bit, turn them around, and **show them the view**: what life looks like with your idea, plus one line that names it.

cards.prompt: Maya just gave a 5-minute talk on why her team should drop the Monday meeting. Which last sentence will people most likely repeat at lunch?

options.text: "That's all from me, thanks so much for listening!"
"Cancel one meeting, and everyone gets their Monday morning back."
"Any questions? Sorry, I know I went a bit over."

whyNot.a: That's a polite exit, not a last line: it carries no idea, so there's nothing to repeat.
whyNot.c: That's handing over the microphone, not reaching the top: the last thing they hear is an apology.

cards.reteach: People can only repeat an ending that has an idea in it. A thank-you or an apology has none. End on a sentence that says your one idea in fresh, short words, and that's what goes home with them.

cards.title: Show them the view
cards.body:
Nancy Duarte, who mapped the shape of famous talks, calls the ending the *new bliss*: a picture of how things look once the audience acts on your idea. Not a recap of what you said. A scene of what changes.

Monday, 9:00, no meeting: the kettle on, an empty calendar, real work starting. That's a view. 'Meetings are inefficient' is just a signpost.

Then comes **one last line that says your one idea again**, short enough to fit on a sticky note. It's the summit you picked in chapter 1, said one final time.
cards.simpler: Nancy Duarte, who studied the shape of famous talks, calls the ending the *new bliss*: a picture of life once people act on your idea. Not a summary, but a scene of what changes. Monday, 9:00, no meeting, the kettle on, real work starting. That is a view. 'Meetings are inefficient' is only a signpost. Then comes **one last line that says your one idea again**, short enough for a sticky note. It's your summit from chapter 1.

cards.title: Two gates, no queue
cards.body: Sam had 5 minutes at the school parents' committee: the car park jams every morning at 8:40, so open the side gate too. His first draft ended: 'So yeah, that's my idea. Thank you!' His second showed the view: 'Picture 8:40 next Monday. Half the cars turn left, nobody's honking, and your kid is inside before the bell.' Then the last line: 'Two gates, no queue.' Three weeks later the committee was saying 'two gates, no queue' about things that had nothing to do with gates.
cards.simpler: Sam had 5 minutes at the school parents' committee: the car park jams at 8:40 every morning, so open the side gate too. His first draft ended: 'So yeah, that's my idea. Thank you!' His second showed the view: 'Picture 8:40 next Monday. Half the cars turn left, nobody's honking, and your kid is inside before the bell.' Then: **'Two gates, no queue.'** Three weeks later the committee used it for things that had nothing to do with gates.

cards.watchFor: Skip to the last stretch of the lecture and notice what he says belongs on the final slide instead of thanks.

cards.prompt: Priya's talk: put savings away on payday, before you can spend them. Which ending reaches the top?

options.text: "To sum up, I covered budgets, apps, interest rates and payday saving."
"Picture opening your bank app in a year and finding a number you forgot you were building. Save on payday, before you can spend it."
"Anyway, I'm out of time, so I'll stop there. Thanks!"

whyNot.a: That's a recap of the trail, not the view: four topics, and the one idea gets lost among them.
whyNot.c: That's stopping below the summit: running out of time isn't an ending, and there's no idea to take home.

cards.reteach: A strong ending has two parts. First a scene of life after the idea, then one short line that says the idea again. A list of everything you covered does neither.

cards.title: The last slide, and three runs
cards.body:
Patrick Winston, who taught MIT's well-known lecture on speaking, had a rule: the final slide is never a thank-you. It stays up through the questions, longer than any other slide, so **put what they got from you there**: your one idea, in your last line's words.

Then rehearse 3 times, out loud, to a timer. Run 1 shows you the trail is too long. Run 2 is for cutting. Run 3 is when the last line comes out without a glance at your notes.

You'd think reading it silently counts. It doesn't: your mouth trips on sentences your eyes glide over.
cards.simpler: Patrick Winston, who taught MIT's well-known lecture on speaking, said the last slide is never a thank-you. It stays up through the questions, longer than any other, so **put what they got from you there**: your one idea, in your last line's words. Then rehearse out loud 3 times, timed. Run 1 shows it's too long. Run 2, you cut. By run 3, the last line comes without notes. Silent reading doesn't count: your mouth trips where your eyes glide.

cards.body: Leo says his last line well, the room goes quiet for two seconds, and he panics: 'Um, so, yeah, that's it, I think, thanks.' Now the mumble is his ending. If you hear yourself say 'so, yeah', you've walked past the summit. **Say the line, then stop**, and let the quiet do its work.
cards.simpler: Leo says his last line well. The room goes quiet for two seconds, and he panics: 'Um, so, yeah, that's it, I think, thanks.' Now the mumble is his ending. If you hear yourself say 'so, yeah', you've walked past the top of the hill. **Say the line, then stop**. The quiet is not a problem. It's the room taking in what you said.

cards.prompt: Your talk is over and one slide stays on screen through ten minutes of questions. What goes on it?

options.text: Your one idea in one sentence, the same words as your last line.
Your email, phone number and three links for further reading.

whyNot.a: That's politeness, not the summit: your longest-showing screen ends up with nothing to take home.
whyNot.c: That's signposts to other trails, not the view from this one: useful, but it pushes your idea off the screen.

cards.reteach: Think of the last slide as the photo people take at the top. It should show the summit: your one idea, in the words of your last line. You can say thanks out loud. The screen is for the idea.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
End a talk by showing people the view, what their life looks like with your idea, then **one short line that says the idea again**, and leave that line on the last slide instead of a thank-you. Rehearse the whole climb 3 times out loud to a timer so the last line comes out clean.

Next: give it to 5 people, and ask 3 what the summit was.
cards.simpler: To end a talk, show people the view: what their life looks like with your idea. Then give **one short line that says the idea again**, and leave that line on the last slide instead of a thank-you. Practise the whole talk 3 times, out loud, with a timer, so the last line comes out clean. Next: give the talk to 5 people, and ask 3 of them what the summit, your one idea, was.

cards.body: Write your talk's last line on a sticky note, 8 words or fewer. Set a 5-minute timer on your phone, say the whole talk out loud once, end on that line, and stop. No thanks.
cards.simpler: Write the last line of your talk on a sticky note, in 8 words or fewer. Set a 5-minute timer on your phone. Say the whole talk out loud once, **end on that line, and stop**. Don't add a thank-you. Let the quiet that follows sit for a moment.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now write a closing line that restates your one idea, and rehearse the full talk 3 times, out loud, to a timer.
